r.정치 구도: A monarchy ruled by the Al Sabah family, but its 1962 constitution gave it the first elected parliament in the Gulf. The 50 members could question ministers and block bills, so parliament often clashed with the cabinet appointed by the ruling family, and dissolutions and fresh elections came again and again. In May 2024 the emir dissolved parliament and suspended parts of the constitution for up to four years, moving lawmaking power to the emir and the cabinet. That was still the case in 2026. Over the same period the government stripped many people of citizenship, often on the grounds that it had been obtained improperly, and in August 2026 a decree took away naturalized citizens' right to vote and run for office. The situation of the Bidoon, stateless residents whose families have lived there for generations, also remains unresolved.

t.why: Iraq invaded in August 1990 and occupied the country for seven months until a US-led coalition drove it out the next year. American forces have been based there in large numbers ever since, and Camp Arifjan became the US Army's logistics hub in the Middle East. For that reason Iranian missiles and drones struck Kuwait several times during the 2026 war between the United States, Israel and Iran, and in June a terminal at the international airport was hit, killing and wounding civilians. Every tanker carrying its crude has to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, and there is no pipeline around it, so a closure cuts off its exports entirely. It wants to develop the offshore Durra gas field with Saudi Arabia, but Iran claims a share and the maritime boundary has never been settled. Kuwait has long acted as a mediator in disputes among Gulf states, including during the 2017 rift with Qatar.
t.rel: Because Iraq to the north invaded it, border and missing-persons issues lingered for a long time. It is close to Saudi Arabia through the Gulf Cooperation Council and disagrees with Iran over the boundary of an offshore gas field.
t.korea: The two countries established diplomatic relations in 1979. Kuwait is one of South Korea's larger crude suppliers, and Korean builders have worked on its infrastructure since the 1970s. The 36 km Sheikh Jaber Causeway across Kuwait Bay was completed in 2019 with Hyundai Engineering & Construction as lead contractor, and the liquefied natural gas import terminal at Al-Zour in the south was built by Hyundai Engineering, Hyundai E&C and Korea Gas Corporation. Incheon International Airport Corporation has operated Terminal 4 at Kuwait International Airport since 2018. When the 2026 war closed the Strait of Hormuz, shipments of Kuwaiti crude to South Korea were affected as well.
t.know: The Kuwaiti dinar is the world's highest-valued currency.
etext: The country is small, but its proven crude reserves are among the largest in the world. Burgan is regarded as the world's second-largest oil field, and it is cheap to produce from. State-owned Kuwait Petroleum Corporation handles everything from drilling and refining to filling stations abroad.

An investment board set up in 1953 to manage oil income grew into today's Kuwait Investment Authority, regarded as the world's oldest sovereign wealth fund. In 1976 it created the Future Generations Fund, which sets aside part of state revenue for the time after oil. When the 2026 war blocked exports, the law was changed so the government could borrow from the fund, the first time since the 1990 occupation.

Exports and state revenue are almost entirely oil. Most citizens work in the public sector, and salaries and subsidies take up a large part of the budget, so a fall in oil prices quickly produces a deficit. Fights between parliament and the government often delayed reforms and big projects, and a law allowing the state to borrow was passed only in 2025. Having the Strait of Hormuz as its only export route was laid bare in the 2026 war.
